maya_vucub_came.name: Summon the living to Xibalba to play the deadly ballgame
maya_vucub_came.notes: With Hun-Came he dispatches the four owl-messengers to summon One and Seven Hunahpu, and later the Hero Twins, to the underworld ballcourt where the houses of ordeal await.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (Christenson trans.), Part Three (Descent of One and Seven Hunahpu; summoning of the Twins)

maya_vucub_came.name: Decree sickness, blood-drawing and bodily decay upon the living
maya_vucub_came.notes: As one of the two paramount Death Lords he presides over the ten subordinate lords of Xibalba whose names are afflictions (Flying Scab, Gathered Blood, Pus Demon, Jaundice Demon, Bone Staff, Skull Staff), causing swelling, wasting and skeletonization of humankind.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (Christenson trans.), Part Three (the Lords of Xibalba and their afflictions)

maya_yum_kaax.name: Guard the wild plants, forest and game animals
maya_yum_kaax.notes: As 'Lord of the Forest' he protects the milpa, wild vegetation and the animals of the bush; farmers and hunters depend on his goodwill and offer him first-fruits and prayers before clearing or hunting.

sources.reference: Karl Taube, The Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan (1992), on God E / the Maize God; Maya ethnography of Yum Kaax

maya_zipacna.name: Wield colossal strength to fell trees and topple houses
maya_zipacna.notes: Single-handedly carries the great house-beam the Four Hundred Boys cannot lift, then collapses their unfinished house upon them as they sleep, killing all; the slain boys rise to the sky as the Pleiades.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (Christenson trans.), Part Two (Zipacna and the Four Hundred Boys)

maya_zipacna.name: Forage the rivers and shores in caiman form
maya_zipacna.notes: A caiman-bodied giant who basks on the beach and hunts fish and crabs in the waterways; his hunger for crab is the lure by which the Hero Twins entomb him beneath a mountain.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (Christenson trans.), Part Two (death of Zipacna by the false crab)

maya_xquic.name: Conceive the Hero Twins from the spittle of a severed head
maya_xquic.notes: At the calabash tree where the head of One Hunahpu is hung, the skull spits into her outstretched hand and she conceives Hunahpu and Xbalanque while still a maiden, becoming the mother-goddess of the Twins.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (Christenson trans.), Part Three (the maiden Lady Blood at the calabash tree)

mende_gbeni.name: Manifest as the chief masked spirit (ngafa) of the Poro society
mende_gbeni.notes: The Gbeni is the paramount masquerade-spirit of the men's Poro society; the masker embodies the bush-spirit and the power (hale) of the society, the masculine counterpart to Sande's Sowo.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Masquerade in Mende culture'; Britannica, 'Poro'

mende_sowo.name: Manifest as the female water-spirit guardian of Sande
mende_sowo.notes: Sowo (sowei) is the tutelary water-spirit of the women's Sande society; the helmet mask incarnates her and is danced by the senior official (ndoli jowei) at the close of girls' initiation. Sande is famously the only African masking tradition performed by women.

sources.reference: Sylvia Ardyn Boone, Radiance from the Waters: Ideals of Feminine Beauty in Mende Art (1986)

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Inana/Ištar' (iconography: goddess upon lion[s])

mesopotamian_adad.name: Storm-god worship at Aleppo and Guzana
mesopotamian_adad.notes: Adad/Ishkur was venerated across Mesopotamia and the Levant; principal cult centres included Aleppo (Halab) and Sikkan/Guzana (biblical Gozan) in northern Syria, where he was invoked as giver of fertilizing rain and dreaded as bringer of the destructive storm.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Iškur/Adad' (cult centres Aleppo, Guzana)

mesopotamian_anu.name: Worship at Uruk (Eanna; later the Bīt Rēš with Antu)
mesopotamian_anu.notes: From the third millennium Anu was worshipped, with interruptions, alongside Inana at the Eanna of Uruk; in the Achaemenid–Seleucid period a new temple, the Bīt Rēš, housed his cult together with his consort Antu, where detailed New-Year ritual texts survive.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'An/Anu' (Eanna; Bīt Rēš with Antu)

mesopotamian_enlil.name: Cult of Enlil at the Ekur of Nippur
mesopotamian_enlil.notes: Enlil's chief sanctuary was the Ekur ('Mountain House') at Nippur, beside the ziggurat called dur-an-ki ('bond of heaven and earth'). As the god who conferred kingship, Mesopotamian rulers travelled to Nippur to have their reigns legitimated; offerings, hymns and the akitu of Ekur renewed cosmic order.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Enlil/Ellil' (Ekur, dur-an-ki, kingship-conferral)

mesopotamian_enki.name: Cult of Ea at the E-abzu of Eridu
mesopotamian_enki.notes: Enki/Ea's principal temple was the E-abzu ('house of the abzu', also E-engur-ra) at Eridu, the oldest cult-place in the Sumerian tradition. Goat-fish and turtle figures and apotropaic incantations belonged to his worship; he was the patron of incantation-priests (āšipu).

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Enki/Ea' (E-abzu at Eridu)

mesopotamian_inanna.name: Cult at the Eanna of Uruk; sacred marriage
mesopotamian_inanna.notes: Inana/Ištar's chief sanctuary was the Eanna ('House of Heaven') at Uruk, also a major economic and administrative complex. Her worship included the sacred-marriage rite, in which the king (as Dumuzi) united with a priestess embodying the goddess to secure fertility and legitimate rule.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Inana/Ištar' (Eanna; sacred marriage)

mesopotamian_dumuzi.name: Mourning for Dumuzi in the month Du'uzu
mesopotamian_dumuzi.notes: In the height of summer, when pasture and crops withered, women across Mesopotamia held public ritual lamentation for the dead shepherd-god Dumuzi/Tammuz; Emesal laments and liturgies in the month Du'uzu mourned his descent and invoked his return. The rite is censured even in Ezekiel 8:14 ('women weeping for Tammuz').

sources.reference: Ezekiel 8:14 (women weeping for Tammuz)
Oracc AMGG, 'Dumuzi/Tammuz'; Babylonian menologies for month Du'uzu

mesopotamian_nanna.name: Cult of the moon-god at the Ekishnugal of Ur
mesopotamian_nanna.notes: Sin/Nanna was tutelary god and divine ruler of Ur, where his temple Ekishnugal and its great ziggurat were repeatedly rebuilt by kings from Ur-Nammu onward; his en-priestesses (such as Enheduanna) served there, and the monthly lunar phases structured the cultic calendar.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Nanna/Suen/Sin' (Ekishnugal at Ur)

mesopotamian_nergal.name: Cult of Nergal at the Emeslam of Kutha
mesopotamian_nergal.notes: Nergal's chief cult centre was Kutha (Tell Ibrahim), home of the temple Emeslam, whence his title Meslamtaea ('he who comes forth from Meslam'). His worship involved offerings to placate the bringer of plague, fire and war.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Nergal' (Emeslam at Kutha; Meslamtaea)

mesopotamian_marduk.name: Akitu (Babylonian New Year) and the Esagila cult
mesopotamian_marduk.notes: Marduk's chief temple was the Esagila in Babylon, with its ziggurat Etemenanki. At the spring akitu the Enuma Elish was recited, the king's authority was renewed before the god, and the statues of Marduk and his son Nabu were carried in procession to the akitu-house and back.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Marduk' (Esagila, Etemenanki, akitu); Babylonian New Year ritual texts

mesopotamian_nabu.name: Cult of Nabu at the Ezida of Borsippa; akitu procession
mesopotamian_nabu.notes: Nabu's principal temple was the Ezida at Borsippa, famed for its libraries and scribal schools. At the Babylonian New Year his statue was conveyed from Borsippa to Babylon to join his father Marduk in the akitu procession.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Nabu' (Ezida at Borsippa; akitu procession)

mesopotamian_ninhursag.name: Cult of the mother-goddess at the Keš sanctuary and Adab
mesopotamian_ninhursag.notes: Ninhursag/Ninmah was worshipped above all at Adab and at Keš, celebrated in the Sumerian 'Keš Temple Hymn'; as midwife of the gods (Nintu, šassūru) she received cult in many cities across millennia.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Mother Goddess (Ninmah, Nintud/r, Belet-ili)'; the Keš Temple Hymn

mesopotamian_ninsun.name: Cult of Ninsun at the Egalmah of Uruk; Ur III royal offerings
mesopotamian_ninsun.notes: Ninsun was worshipped at Uruk (her temple Egalmah in the Epic of Gilgamesh) and elsewhere; as divine mother claimed by the Ur III kings she and Lugalbanda received offerings at Nippur on several lunar festivals and at Uruk into the Old Babylonian period.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Ninsumun (Ninsun)' (Egalmah; Ur III offerings with Lugalbanda)

mesopotamian_gilgamesh.name: Invocation in funerary ritual as judge of the netherworld
mesopotamian_gilgamesh.cadence: funerary; festival of the dead (month Abu)
mesopotamian_gilgamesh.notes: In the first millennium Gilgamesh was invoked in funerary rites as a deity of the underworld and judge of the dead ('O Gilgamesh, perfect king, judge of the Anunnaki'); at the festival of the ghosts in month Abu no light was offered to the dead without him.

sources.reference: ETCSL 1.8.1.3, 'The Death of Bilgames'; first-millennium prayers to Gilgamesh of the dead

mesopotamian_geshtinanna.name: Cult of Geshtinanna at Sagub in Lagaš
mesopotamian_geshtinanna.notes: Evidence for her worship is clearest in the Early Dynastic state of Lagaš, where she held her own cult centre at Sagub; she was honoured as scribe and record-keeper of the netherworld (Belet-seri) and as the sister who took Dumuzi's place below.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Geštinanna/Belet-ṣeri' (cult at Sagub, Lagaš)

mesopotamian_shulgi.name: Royal cult of the deified living king
mesopotamian_shulgi.notes: From around his twenty-first year Šulgi wrote his name with the divine determinative dingir and instituted a state cult of the living king: cult-statues received regular offerings, temples and festivals were dedicated to him, months were named for those festivals, and his name entered personal names as a theophoric element.

sources.reference: P. Michalowski and Ur III studies on the cult of the deified king; Šulgi royal hymns

mesopotamian_amar_sin.name: Royal cult of the deified king
mesopotamian_amar_sin.notes: Continuing the Šulgi-period practice, Amar-Sin wrote his name with the divine determinative and received cult as a living god; he also built a temple to Enki at Eridu.

sources.reference: Ur III studies on the deified-king cult; Amar-Sin royal inscriptions

mesopotamian_shu_sin.name: Royal cult of the deified king; sacred-marriage love songs
mesopotamian_shu_sin.notes: Šu-Sin was worshipped as a living god (his name written with the divine determinative; a temple to him excavated at Eshnunna) and figures as the bridegroom Dumuzi in a cycle of Sumerian sacred-marriage love songs addressed to him.

sources.reference: Ur III studies on the deified-king cult; the Šu-Sin love songs (ETCSL 2.4.4)

maya_yum_kaax.name: First-fruit offerings of farmers and hunters
maya_yum_kaax.notes: As patron of the milpa and the forest, Yum Kaax received prayers and offerings of first harvests and was propitiated by hunters seeking his protection over the game and wild plants of the bush.

sources.reference: Maya ethnography of Yum Kaax (Lord of the Forest); Taube, Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan (1992)

maya_xmucane.name: Invocation of the divine grandparents by the daykeepers (aj qʼij)
maya_xmucane.notes: As the primordial diviner-grandmother (with Xpiacoc) Xmucane is invoked by name at the opening of K'iche' divination; the highland Guatemalan daykeeper (aj qʼij) tradition still calls on 'our grandmother, our grandfather' when casting lots with maize and tzité (coral-tree) seeds.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (Christenson trans.), Part One (invocation of Xpiyacoc and Xmucane); Part Four (the maize grinding)

maya_xpiacoc.name: Invocation of the divine grandparents by the daykeepers (aj qʼij)
maya_xpiacoc.notes: The diviner-grandfather of the Popol Vuh, consulted by the makers Tepeu and Gucumatz to read the lots; the K'iche' daykeeper tradition of Momostenango and Chichicastenango still invokes Xpiacoc-Xmucane when divining with maize grains and tzité seeds.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (Christenson trans.), Part One (the diviners cast lots with corn and tzité)

mende_gbeni.name: Poro masquerade: initiation and law-enforcement
mende_gbeni.notes: The Gbeni and lesser Poro maskers appear at the initiation of boys (a withdrawal into a secluded forest grove) and enforce communal law, also presiding at the coronations and funerals of chiefs and society officials.

sources.reference: Britannica, 'Poro'; Wikipedia, 'Masquerade in Mende culture'

mende_sowo.name: Sande masquerade at girls' initiation
mende_sowo.notes: The sowei mask is danced by the ndoli jowei to mark the close of the girls' Sande initiation, when novices emerge from seclusion having been instructed in the ideals of Mende womanhood; the dancer is regarded as the bride of the male water-spirit dwelling in the mask.

sources.reference: Boone, Radiance from the Waters (1986); Smarthistory, 'Bundu/Sowei Helmet Mask'

mende_ngewo.name: Approach to the high god through ancestors and lesser spirits
mende_ngewo.notes: Ngewo (older name Leve, 'the high-up one') is the remote creator who set the world in order and withdrew; the Mende do not address him with a temple cult directly but reach him through the Poro and Sande societies, the ancestors, and the lesser tutelary spirits (ngafanga).

sources.reference: Encyclopedia of African Religion (2009), 'Ngewo'; Britannica, 'Mende'

attributes.name: Mounted on or beside the lion-dragon and the bull
attributes.notes: In third-millennium art the storm-god's beast is the lion-dragon; from the Ur III period the bull (whose bellow equals thunder) predominates. Assyrian reliefs (e.g. the Arslan Tash stela) show Adad astride a bull brandishing forked lightning.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Iškur/Adad' (lion-dragon, bull, lightning-fork)
Oracc AMGG, 'Iškur/Adad' (the bull as storm-god's animal)

attributes.name: Seated god with twin water-streams flowing from his shoulders
attributes.notes: Customarily shown bearded, in a horned cap and pleated robe, with wavy streams of water (often containing fish) flowing from his arms and shoulders to the ground.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Enki/Ea' (flowing-water iconography)
Oracc AMGG, 'Enki/Ea' (the goat-fish suhurmašu)
Oracc AMGG, 'Enki/Ea' (turtle among his symbols)

attributes.name: Triangular spade (marru) emblem
attributes.notes: Marduk's defining symbol is the marru, a triangular-headed spade, inherited from the farmer-god Asalluhi with whom he was identified.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Marduk' (the marru/spade)
Oracc AMGG, 'Marduk'; the Ishtar Gate of Babylon (mušḫuššu of Marduk)

attributes.name: Single wedge (stylus) upon a writing-tablet or dais
attributes.notes: Nabu's symbol is a single cuneiform wedge, vertical or horizontal, sometimes shown resting on a clay tablet, representing the scribe's stylus.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Nabu' (the wedge/stylus on a tablet)
Oracc AMGG, 'Nabu' (rides the mušḫuššu)

attributes.name: Seated god with a long beard of lapis lazuli beneath a crescent
attributes.notes: Depicted as a seated man with a flowing lapis-lazuli beard and a crescent moon above him, or riding a winged bull; most often represented simply by the crescent.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Nanna/Suen/Sin' (lapis beard, crescent, winged bull)
Oracc AMGG, 'Nanna/Suen/Sin' (the bull, by the crescent-horn association)

attributes.name: Striding warrior bearing scimitar and lion-headed mace
attributes.notes: Portrayed as an armed striding figure carrying a scimitar or a mace topped with a double lion's head, attended by his demon retinue.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Nergal' (scimitar and lion-headed mace)
Oracc AMGG, 'Nergal' (lion as his animal)
Oracc AMGG, 'An/Anu' (the bull as Anu's animal)

attributes.name: Omega-shaped birth emblem with horned headdress
attributes.notes: Identified by the omega-shaped symbol (read as a stylized uterus or coiled hair), a horned headdress, and at times a mace, marking her as womb-goddess and midwife of the gods.

sources.reference: Oracc AMGG, 'Mother Goddess (Ninmah, Nintud/r, Belet-ili)' (omega emblem)

attributes.name: Death-lord of Xibalba
attributes.notes: One of the two paramount lords of the Maya underworld, his name '7-Death' marking him as a calendrical death-deity who presides over the houses of ordeal and the lethal ballcourt.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (Christenson trans.), Part Three (Hun-Came and Vucub-Came, lords of Xibalba)
Popol Vuh (Christenson trans.), Part Three (the owl-messengers of the Death Lords)

attributes.name: False sun with metal beak and jeweled teeth
attributes.notes: A great macaw with brilliant red plumage who perches in a nance tree and falsely proclaims himself sun and moon; he flaunts a shining metal beak and teeth of jade and gemstone, and is brought down by the Hero Twins' blowgun.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (Christenson trans.), Part Two (Seven Macaw the false sun)
Popol Vuh (Christenson trans.), Part Two (Seven Macaw in the nance tree)

attributes.name: Youthful god with an elongated head and maize-cob headdress
attributes.notes: Schellhas's God E: eternally youthful, his cranium elongated to a maize-ear, crowned with a foliated or corn-cob headdress and the Kan ('maize') sign, embodying the growing and resurrected maize.

sources.reference: Karl Taube, The Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan (1992), God E / the Maize God
Taube, Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan (1992) (the maize god and the maize plant)

attributes.name: Caiman-bodied raiser of mountains
attributes.notes: A boastful giant in the form of a caiman, son of the false sun Vucub Caquix and Chimalmat, who claims to make and carry the mountains; entombed beneath a mountain by the Hero Twins' false-crab ruse.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (Christenson trans.), Part Two (Zipacna the caiman)
Popol Vuh (Christenson trans.), Part Two (Zipacna in caiman form)

attributes.name: Maiden of the calabash tree and the croton-resin heart
attributes.notes: Lady Blood, daughter of the Xibalba lord Cuchumaquic; she conceives the Twins at the skull-bearing calabash tree and escapes the underworld by substituting congealed red croton-tree resin for her own heart, deceiving the death-owls sent to kill her.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (Christenson trans.), Part Three (Lady Blood, the calabash tree and the croton sap)
Popol Vuh (Christenson trans.), Part Three (the calabash tree bearing the skull)

attributes.name: Black lustrous helmet mask with ringed neck and downcast features
attributes.notes: The sowei mask realizes the Mende ideal of feminine beauty: a dark, glossy (water-wet) surface; a high broad forehead; small, serene features with downcast eyes and a closed mouth (modesty and self-possession); and rings of flesh at the neck signifying health, fecundity and prosperity; worn with a voluminous raffia costume.

sources.reference: Boone, Radiance from the Waters (1986); Smarthistory, 'Bundu/Sowei Helmet Mask'
